20696-highways-and-byways-in-sussex:
Highways and Byways in Sussex is a travel book in the beloved Highways and Byways series, which walked readers county by county through England. Its Sussex volume crosses the Downs, the coast towns, and the weald between. Anecdote and history season every mile of the road.

The Downs give Sussex its unique character, the writer says. Their virginal security and unassailable independence set them apart. They stand, a silent undiscovered country, between the seething pleasure towns of the seaboard plain and the trim estates inland. The book teaches readers to see that quiet country as its lovers did.
22328-oh-you-tex:
William MacLeod Raine wrote Oh, You Tex!, a western novel of the open desert. Its hero, Jack Roberts, starts the story fifty miles from nowhere. Alone, he dances to a tin cup beaten against a tin plate.

Youth, Raine writes, set his feet to moving. Jack is twenty-one, five feet eleven, and solidly built. He carries one hundred seventy pounds of bone, sinew, and muscle. That cheerful opening tells readers what kind of hero to expect. Raine filled westerns with riders, ranches, and quick action. Tex gives that formula a likable start, with a young cowboy happy even in empty country.

nasa-tm-19700017991-ephemeris-of-a-highl:
Barbara E. Lowrey of the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint in May 1970. It gives an ephemeris for Explorer 28, also called IMP 3, a satellite in a highly eccentric orbit. An ephemeris is a table that lists where an object will be at set times.

Lowrey's ephemeris matched two years of radio observations well and stayed close to optical observations a year later. It was built by numerical integration from launch conditions, with no later correction passes. She improved the starting conditions by matching computed perigee times against observed ones. Because such orbits are hard to compute, the long matched arc can serve as a standard for other work.
sex-and-society-studies-in-the-social-ps:
William I. Thomas, associate professor of sociology at the University of Chicago, gathered these studies in 1907; a fourth impression followed in 1913. The pieces first ran in journals at scattered dates. Thomas revised and in places expanded them for the book, by request of readers who found them hard to reach.

One thesis runs through the set: bodily habits differ by sex, with men stronger, more restless, and more apt for motion, women more settled. Thomas traces how that gap shaped social forms, work, morals, and mind. Studies treat early social control, early industry, modesty, and related themes in turn.
the-descent-of-man-and-selection-in-rela:
Charles Darwin's The Descent of Man and Selection in Relation to Sex is laid out in three parts. Part I treats the descent or origin of man, the proof of his rise from some lower form. It compares his mental powers with those of lower animals, and treats the races of man. Parts II and III turn to sexual selection, tracing secondary sexual characters in insects, fishes, birds, and mammals, and then in man himself.

A preface to the second edition explains that, through the reprints of the first edition, published in 1871, Darwin was able to introduce several important corrections. With more time passed, he has now profited by the fiery ordeal the book went through, taking up every criticism that seems to him sound. Many correspondents, he adds, sent a surprising store of new facts and remarks, of which he could use only the more important.
the-discovery-of-yellowstone-park-journa:
Nathaniel Pitt Langford's The Discovery of Yellowstone Park, dated 1905, presents his journal of the Washburn Expedition to the Yellowstone and Firehole Rivers in the year 1870. A contents note lists a foreword and index not included here. A portrait of James Bridger stands near the front.

Langford opens on the mountaineers of Montana, reputed fabricators who loved practicing on the credulity of their listeners. Bridger, discoverer of Great Salt Lake, wove so much romance around his Indian adventures that hearers took them with many grains of allowance. Once, near Pumpkin Butte by Fort Laramie, a young attache asked if he had lived long on the plains. Bridger pointed at the butte, a thousand feet above the plain, and said that mountain was a hole in the ground when he came here. Bridger's mountain life began in 1820, and by 1832 he was a resident partner in the Rocky Mountain Fur Company.
